question: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.

raiseTranscript.text: I had to push back on a feature request from my manager because the data showed it would break our core metrics. I ran the analysis, presented the trade-offs, and we shipped a smaller scoped version instead.
The PM wanted it for a customer demo. I stuck with the data and owned the decision through launch.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: new grad on search team, 9 months in
Situation: PM wanted quick feature for demo; data showed regression in relevance
Action: ran A/B analysis, presented trade-offs to manager, scoped down
Outcome: shipped smaller version, metrics held; quote: 'I owned the decision through launch'
Follow-up: How did you handle pushback? - 'I asked for their concerns and showed the numbers again'
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for junior level. Candidate described owning a data-driven call on their own work despite manager pressure. They scoped the feature after analysis and stayed with the decision through launch. The concrete trade-off shown was relevance metrics versus demo timeline. This demonstrates local ownership and willingness to surface evidence rather than defer. Biggest strength is clear articulation of why the decision was made and how they stood by it without escalation.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager told me to change the priority of a bug I was fixing. I disagreed but did it anyway because they were the manager.
It delayed my other work but I just followed the instruction.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: new grad, 8 months
Situation: manager reprioritized bug fix
Action: followed instruction without further input
Outcome: work delayed; no evidence of judgment applied
Follow-up: What would you do differently? - 'Probably the same'
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for junior level. The candidate described deferring entirely to authority with no analysis or pushback shown. They accepted the reprioritization without surfacing trade-offs or data. The story stays at the level of following instructions rather than exercising judgment on their own work. No ownership of the outcome is demonstrated. Biggest gap is absence of any decision the candidate themselves made or defended.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams disagreed on API contract changes that would affect performance. I decided to keep the existing contract and invest in a caching layer instead, even though the other team wanted the change for their roadmap.
I showed cross-team latency data and ran a small prototype. Both teams agreed after seeing the numbers.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: senior on platform team, cross-team impact
Situation: API change request from consuming team threatened latency SLOs
Action: analyzed data, proposed caching alternative, prototyped
Outcome: contract unchanged, latency held; quote: 'showed cross-team latency data'
Follow-up: What if they had escalated? - 'I would have asked for a joint review with the data'
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for senior level. Candidate made a call that affected another team and defended the existing contract using data and a prototype. The decision protected a shared SLO while still addressing the other team's needs through an alternative. Influence happened without authority via evidence rather than escalation. The story shows measurable cross-team impact. Biggest strength is balancing technical trade-offs across boundaries with clear ownership of the outcome.

lowerTranscript.text: I recommended against a design change but the other team went ahead anyway. I documented my concerns and moved on.
Did you try to influence the outcome?
I sent an email with my analysis but didn't follow up after that.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: senior engineer
Situation: design disagreement with peer team
Action: sent analysis email then dropped it
Outcome: change shipped despite concerns; no further action
Follow-up: What was the result? - 'They shipped and it was fine'
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for senior level. The candidate surfaced concerns once via email but showed no sustained effort to influence the cross-team decision. They accepted the outcome without further data or escalation attempts. The story lacks evidence of standing by a judgment when it mattered. No metrics or follow-through are described. Biggest gap is treating influence as a one-time notification rather than active ownership across teams.

raiseTranscript.text: I had to move a strong performer off a high-visibility project because the team needed their skills elsewhere. The individual and their current lead both pushed back hard.
How did you handle the pushback?
I explained the team-level impact, offered a clear timeline for return, and checked in weekly with the person to keep them engaged.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: engineering manager, team of 8
Situation: reassign key person from visible project to cover critical gap
Action: made call, explained trade-offs, set return timeline, weekly 1:1s
Outcome: project delivered, person retained and promoted later; quote: 'offered a clear timeline for return'
Follow-up: What was the business impact? - 'Avoided two-week slip on another launch'
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for manager level. Candidate made a people decision that protected overall team delivery despite resistance from the individual and peer lead. They owned the trade-off, communicated it directly, and followed through with ongoing support. The outcome included both project success and retention of the person. This shows leverage through team allocation rather than heroics. Biggest strength is balancing individual impact with org-level needs while maintaining transparency.

lowerTranscript.text: I reassigned someone because my director asked me to. The team was unhappy but I told them it was above my pay grade.
How did you support the person?
I let them know it was temporary and moved on to other work.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: engineering manager
Situation: forced reassignment from director
Action: relayed decision without adding context or support
Outcome: team unhappy; no evidence of manager ownership
Follow-up: What happened to the person? - 'They left six months later'
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for manager level. The candidate treated the reassignment as something handed down rather than a decision they owned. They provided minimal support and no visible effort to mitigate team impact. The story shows no attempt to shape the outcome or develop the affected person. Long-term result was attrition. Biggest gap is absence of manager-level accountability for team health and delivery trade-offs.

raiseTranscript.text: We had to sunset a product line that was still generating revenue because it was blocking a larger platform bet. The sales team was strongly opposed.
We modeled the platform opportunity versus continued revenue and set a six-month wind-down with customer transition support. I personally briefed the top accounts.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: VP, org of 200+
Situation: revenue-generating product conflicting with strategic platform direction
Action: modeled trade-offs, set wind-down plan, briefed key customers directly
Outcome: platform launched on time, net revenue impact neutral after two quarters
Follow-up: How did you handle sales pushback? - 'I owned the narrative in every account review'
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for exec level. Candidate made a high-ambiguity call to sunset revenue to unlock a larger strategic bet. They modeled the long-term trade-off, owned the customer communication, and accepted short-term revenue pressure. The outcome showed disciplined execution with measurable platform impact. This reflects strategic judgment over local optimization. Biggest strength is willingness to make an org-level trade-off and personally absorb the resulting friction.

lowerTranscript.text: We kept the product running because sales said it would hurt the quarter. I agreed it was the safer call.
We delayed the platform work by nine months and lost two key engineering hires.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you had to make an unpopular or difficult decision and stand by it.
Role: VP
Situation: product line conflicting with platform strategy
Action: deferred to sales input and kept product alive
Outcome: platform delayed, talent loss; no strategic decision made
Follow-up: What would you do now? - 'Probably the same to protect revenue'
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Decision Making & Judgment for exec level. The candidate avoided the difficult call by prioritizing short-term revenue signals over the strategic platform direction. No modeling of long-term trade-offs is shown. The result was delayed execution and talent attrition. The story reflects risk aversion rather than strategic ownership. Biggest gap is failure to make a clear decision when ambiguity and stakeholder resistance were high.

diagnostic.junior: Owns local technical call with data

diagnostic.senior: Uses prototype and data for influence
diagnostic.manager: Sets timeline and follows up with person
